content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper reports an investigation of the problem of human-to-robot policy transfer for object manipulation tasks. The work proposes to use visual observations of human demonstrations collected from a hand-centric point of view. To avoid over-fitting to the visual appearance of the human or robot hand, RGB observations are cropped zeroing out the top part of the image, hence excluding the human or robotic hand from the observations. The paper reports experiments to show the advantage in terms of environment and task generalization of using both human and robot demonstrations for training, as well as the effect of cropping visual observations.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer xd3t
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer xd3t,

Thank you so much for your helpful and well-communicated review. We appreciate that you found the paper well-written and easy to follow, and that you thought the idea and setup are interesting and easily applicable to many contexts. In addition, we appreciate that you mentioned several ways in which we could improve the paper. We respond to individual points below.

> The paper states that egocentric and third person human demonstration provide suboptimal data. However, this statement is never assessed experimentally. I would have expected to see experiments comparing third person data vs egocentric data vs hand-centric data vs cropped hand-centric data. In the lack of these experiments it's hard to verify these claims.

Indeed, our experiments are focused on the hand-centric camera setting and omit other settings, such as third-person, but this is rather intentional. This is because past works have already completed extensive empirical analysis comparing the hand-centric and third-person camera settings, including the work titled “Look Closer: Bridging Egocentric and Third-Person Views with Transformers for Robotic Manipulation” by Jangir and Hansen et al. (RA-L 2022) and “Vision-Based Manipulators Need to Also See from Their Hands” by Hsu and Kim et al. (ICLR 2022). We believe that the findings in these works would apply in our setup as well, so we focus on the hand-centric setting and see what gains we can achieve there by leveraging human demonstrations. We also note that we do include a comparison between cropped and uncropped hand-centric data in Section 5.4 of the paper.

> The proposed approach is not compared with respect to any prior work tackling human to robot policy transfer. I am referring in particular to the works mentioned in Section "2 Related Work", e.g., (Liu et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2019), (Smith et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2021), or even just CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017).

The prior works utilize the third-person camera perspective and often state different sets of assumptions, but we are looking forward to comparing against works that can be incorporated into the hand-centric setting, such as CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017) for human-to-robot image translation. Thank you for the suggestion.

> Even if the proposed approach is learning from human demonstrations, these are still performed in constrained settings in a lab with similar visual appearance. Indeed, the actual variations between environment changes do not always reflect realistic conditions (e.g., see Figure 4).

For the environment generalization experiments, we intended to cover a diverse set of visual variations, including varying distractor objects (in the reaching task), varying environment backgrounds (in the grasping task), and varying target objects (in the plate clearing task). However, we appreciate your input and are looking forward to conducting future experiments with more realistic settings to further strengthen the results.

Thank you again for all your inputs and suggestions on how we could strengthen this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to do imitation learning from hand-centric videos. The authors describe the setting of hand-centric video recording, and benchmark the setting with behavior cloning tasks, and also showcase the generalization on both environment configuration and task horizons with addition of human dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The paper is well-written, and well-motivated.

2. The hand-centric setting is a clever setup to record the demonstration videos with less domain gap.

Weakness:

1. The action space of robot is 4 dimension, 3 dofs for end-effector position and 1 dof for gripper. I wonder what does the 3 dofs represent? Even if the gripper is operated in a top-down fashion, it should consider (x,y,z) and a rotation angle. I am not sure which dimension can be neglected in this setting? If the rotation angle is omitted, will not the robot action be rather too easy?

2. The limit in action space of gripper actually raises another issue, will the hand-centric recording still work when the gripper approach in SO(3) with 6DOFs? That means if the gripper approaches in a tilt angle, the visible region in the hand-centric camera will be much less. 

3. I think the paper misuse the term of “inverse dynamics”. The inverse dynamics is to calculate the force/torque on the joints from the kinematics. But in the context of this paper, the inverse model inputs the observation and output the action, which has nothing to do with joint force/torque.

4. After the imitation model trained from the gripper actions, it is applied to human data. I wonder how accurate is the prediction of actions? It seems no quantitative results, or verification mechanism to ensure this. If the prediction already very precise, does human demonstration really provide additional information? If the prediction is not very precise, then how to exploit the labels with noise? I can imagine the human data will bring more information to facilitate the generalization, but it should be carefully discussed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality: The idea of hand-centric setup is interesting, but I see many limitations, e.g. 2-finger gripper in SO(3), multi-finger robot hands.
Clarity: The paper is well-written and easily to follow
Novelty: The setup is novel to me, but the benchmark is rather easy.
Reproducibility: It seems rather easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review:

3. There are come claims should be made clearer, e.g. gripper action space, inverse dynamics model.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer fR5A
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer fR5A,

Thank you so much for your thorough review. We appreciate that you found the paper well-written and well-motivated, and that you deemed the setup to be clever. We also appreciate that you brought forth clear ways in which we can strengthen the paper. We respond to individual points below.

> The action space of robot is 4 dimension, 3 dofs for end-effector position and 1 dof for gripper. I wonder what does the 3 dofs represent?

The 3 DoFs represent (x,y,z) position control. Changing the end-effector’s rotation angle is currently not included in the action space.

> If the rotation angle is omitted, will not the robot action be rather too easy?

We show in the paper real-world tasks of varying complexity which can be completed with our current 3-DoF position control actions (with an additional DoF for the gripper action). While certain tasks such as reaching may indeed be easy, we observe that the robot still generalizes poorly in such a simple task and show how our framework for using human demonstrations can significantly improve the performance there. Other tasks, such as cube stacking, pick-and-place, and plate clearing, are longer-horizon and nontrivial but can still be solved with 3-DoF position control. However, we are open to extending the results to the 6-DoF action space in the future.

> The limit in action space of gripper actually raises another issue, will the hand-centric recording still work when the gripper approach in SO(3) with 6DOFs?

Yes, our framework would still apply given a 6-DoF action space since the position and orientation of the manipulator is agnostic to the agent’s embodiment.

> I think the paper misuse the term of “inverse dynamics”.

We are using the term “inverse dynamics model” in the same fashion as the five works cited in Section 4.2 of our paper (Nair et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Schmeckpeper et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). This term is overloaded and has more than one definition, including the one that you described regarding joint forces/torques. We will revise the paper to clarify this.

> I can imagine the human data will bring more information to facilitate the generalization, but it should be carefully discussed.

We agree that the paper would benefit from additional discussion of the inverse model predictions on human data and are looking forward to incorporating this in the future.

Thank you again for providing detailed feedback for this work.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer osZk
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer osZk,

Thank you so much for your thoughtful review. We appreciate that you mentioned positive aspects of the paper (such as its comprehensiveness, clarity, quality, and reproducibility) while also providing feedback that helps us improve the paper. We respond to individual points below.

> Also, the whole idea of manually cropping out the hand and end-effctor seems to be a tedious task if a diverse range of scenarious needs to be considered.

We would like to clarify that the cropping of the hand and end-effector from the images is done automatically—not manually—as every image is cropped in exactly the same way with a script. Concretely, the script simply blacks out the top 36% of every image, e.g., via `img[:,:36,:] = 0` given an RGB image with shape (3,100,100). Since this process is simple and automated, it is actually not tedious at all, even when a diverse range of scenarios is considered. We added a note to the paper to clarify this.

> The occlusion challenge posed during the action recording still exists and it is very unclear on how these kind of depth related issues are addressed while using the RGB camera.

Cropping the images indeed leads to some occlusion, which is a limitation we address in Section 6 of the paper (Conclusion). However, as shown by the experiments, we are still able to complete various tasks with marked improvement in generalization performance, using only RGB images and without needing explicit depth information.

> There seems to be less significant contributions and novelty as the paper proposes a RGB camera based action recording and a manual cropping procedure.

We believe that the main contributions of this paper arise precisely from the simplicity of our framework, which makes it easy to apply to other robotic systems while also allowing for significant gains in generalization performance. To our knowledge, this work marks the first time that a real robot policy has been successfully trained end-to-end on hand-centric human demonstrations.

> Although authors claim to have a broder impact in terms of generalized performance, a lot more challenging aspects seems to be missing out.

We believe that the ability of robotic manipulators to generalize to various new environments and new tasks, as shown in our experiments conducted in the real world, indeed show potential for broader impact in terms of generalization. We appreciate your feedback and are looking forward to adding more challenging tasks in the future to convey the extent to which our framework could be applied and be useful.

Thank you again for your time and effort in reviewing our work.
